Photograph: Martin Pope/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Protests have been held over plans to house asylum seekers on the RAF Barnham site near Thetford. Photograph: Martin Pope/Getty Images UK news Norfolk police arrest two men after officers injured during unrest over asylum plans Homes of people believed to be asylum seekers attacked during two nights of violence in Thetford Matthew Weaver Thu 6 Aug 2026 14.06 EDT Last modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 18.39 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Two men have been arrested after police were injured as they intervened to protect men believed to be asylum seekers from angry mobs trying to break into their homes. The arrests followed two nights of unrest in Thetford, Norfolk, involving more than 100 people protesting against plans to house asylum seekers in former military barracks near the market town. The unrest followed the circulation online of a list of properties whose landlords have contracts with a government contractor to provide homes for asylum seekers. Policing powers in Norfolk were boosted in Thetford on Thursday evening and public safety measures have been imposed. Norfolk police said on Wednesday one of its officers was struck by a rock, another officer was bitten and a third was spat at while responding to reports of protesters trying to break into a home in the north of the town. The injured officers were taken to hospital. One man in his 40s, who was arrested on suspected public order offences, remains in custody. A second man, Brian Thompson, 68, has been charged with possession of an offensive weapon, a wooden bat. He is due to appear at Norwich magistrates court on 25 August. View image in fullscreen Damage caused to a house in Thetford where protesters allegedly tried to break into the homes of people believed to be asylum seekers. Photograph: Joe Giddens/PA On Tuesday night, officers intervened to protect five men who were being threatened by dozens of protesters, some of whom tried to break into a property, smashed a window, and damaged a fence and letterbox. Police were responding to a report that between 30 and 50 people were trying to enter a house in the west of Thetford. Video footage of the incident showed the men being escorted to safety by officers as dozens of protesters jeered and shouted abuse at police and the men. Shouts of “refugees not welcome”, “get out” and “bye” could be heard. In another video of the unrest, a man could be heard shouting: “They don’t want the white man any more, they want to swap us.” Later on Tuesday, officers responded to reports of residents being threatened at two homes in the south of the town. Police believed some of those involved had been present at the earlier attempted break-in. At one of the homes, windows were smashed. At another, a resident was forced out and had their mobile phone stolen when a small group forced entry. A man in his 30s who was arrested over Tuesday’s night’s unrest on suspicion of a public order offence had since been released and issued with a conditional caution, police said. The local Labour MP, Terry Jermy, who has previously criticised plans to use the former barracks at nearby RAF Barnham to house up to 1,000 asylum seekers, condemned the violence and what he called “mob rule”. View image in fullscreen The arrests followed two nights of unrest in Thetford involving more than 100 people protesting against plans to house asylum seekers at the RAF Barnham site (pictured). Photograph: Martin Pope/Getty Images Jermy said protesters were targeting a list of houses of multiple occupation used by Serco to house asylum seekers. “There doesn’t seem to be protests at all of the properties known about thus far, so the potential for increase and escalation is clearly there,” he said. “I’ve had constituents contact me of mixed ethnicity who are terrified that they will be misidentified as asylum seekers and what that might mean for their families.” Jermy said he recognised many of the protesters as local people in the videos of the unrest, but that he believed tensions were being “whipped up by outside forces”. In a statement, Jermy said: “The ugly scenes in Thetford over the past few days have been difficult to watch and are deeply concerning. “People have been pulled from their homes – a place of safety – and forcibly removed, with reports of members of the public breaking into homes, taking property and smashing windows. “I do not know the immigration status of the people placed in these properties or their legal status, but I know they are human beings that must be afforded the same rights that we all expect in this country. “Whatever our own individual views on immigration – mob rule and vigilantism is not acceptable.” View image in fullscreen Under the proposals, the RAF Barnham site could house 1,000 asylum seekers. Photograph: Martin Pope/Getty Images Norfolk police also condemned the violence. The assistant chief constable Julie Dean, who is overseeing the response to the unrest, said: “We will always facilitate and support the right to peaceful protest. However, no matter how strongly those views are held, there is no place for violence, intimidation or criminal behaviour. “We will not stand by and allow violence to take place, whether that is directed towards members of the public, local residents or police officers carrying out their duties.” Policing powers in Norfolk were increased in Thetford on Thursday evening. Public safety measures have been imposed, including people being required to remove a face covering if asked to do so by officers. Police will also be permitted to direct anyone committing, or whom they suspect may commit, antisocial behaviour to leave the area. The measures are in place from 6pm on Thursday until 7am on Friday. Anyone who refuses to remove a face covering when asked to do so may be arrested, the force said. https://www.budapesttimes.hu/people/when.text: The Budapest Times When Carlos the Jackal hid out in in Cold War Hungary Written by Alexander Stemp Following on from my article last year about the three “Hungarian Jackals” involved in the assassination attempt on President of France Charles de Gaulle in 1962, now comes the tale of another “Jackal” connection, this time Carlos the Jackal, the internationally hunted terrorist and his secret hideout in the select Budapest suburb Rózsadomb from 1979 to 1985. It still remains a mystery why Hungary allowed entry to this notorious figure sought over a series of assassinations and terrorist acts. Certainly, hosting the committed Marxist-Leninist earned the goodwill of the Communist and anti -Western world that generally supported him in defiance of mounting pressure from the West to bring him to justice, wherever he was holed up. The Hungarian authorities have not released his files and it is not known where he lived at leafy “Rose Hill”, but presumably in a nice enough villa. While it was prepared the Jackal briefly stayed at the cosmopolitan and five-star Hotel Intercontinental, today named the Marriott, a cubist structure in central Pest overlooking the River Danube. Both the hotel and the nearby monumental Inter-Continental “glass-house”, which opened in 1968, were symbols of the more progressive and prosperous Hungarian “Goulash Communism”, designed to attract the rich and famous from around the world. Everyone and everything came and went, with this newish riverside setting an obvious clandestine location for Eastern and Western diplomats, journalists, artists, prostitutes and spies during the Socialist Cold War era. Such premises were heavily bugged, having surveillance cameras, hidden microphones, discreet observers and so forth. Despite the precariousness, the hotels also served as a checkpoint where the Hungarian regime permitted various forms of contact between East and West, while still keeping tabs on one another. The Jackal remained able to carry on his illicit activities. Carlos the Jackal’s real name was Ilich Ramírez Sánchez and he was Venezuelan, born into a privileged family in 1949. Educated in Caracas, London and Moscow, he underwent guerrilla training in the Middle East, playing an active role for the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine and gaining a reputation as a fighter. He travelled around Europe and the Middle East, and led the 1975 raid on the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries headquarters in Vienna. This ended in his demanding a plane and successfully flying with hostages to Libya. Eventually he made his way to Hungary, where the authorities maintained fairly amicable relations with both East and West throughout the Cold War. Hungary was playing safe with the USSR and keeping friendly with the various anti-Western countries favourable to Carlos. While the Jackal reposed in low-profile comfort, he remained a concern and was always very closely watched by the Hungarian Secret Police. The secretive Hungarian authorities naturally kept the matter under wraps and away from the outside world. Carlos remained relatively safe on Hungarian territory and was not called upon for any services by President János Kádár. Hosts and guest basically left each another alone. But eventually his presence became an uncomfortable matter for Hungary, an irritant affecting foreign relations and the delicate balance of geopolitics. It was clear that he had overstayed his time and must go. Finally, under international pressure especially from the United States due to his continual anti-Israeli activities, he was expelled in late 1985. Hungary wanted more open relations with the West, and while it was a tricky move to expel him there was relief too. At least the country could report to the Soviets and to the rest of the world what an uncontrollable and unpredictable person he was. The “Jackal” left without issues and travelled to Syria but later was chased out. When the Cold War ended in 1989 he fled to Sudan and was finally captured by French military agents in Khartoum in 1994. Sentenced to a high-security prison in Paris, he is still serving life sentences in France today. To round off, I know nothing about how the “Carlos” part of his nickname evolved but he was dubbed “The Jackal” by The Guardian, a British newspaper, after one of its investigative correspondents reportedly found Frederick Forsyth’s 1971 novel “The Day of the Jackal” in an apartment belonging to a friend of Carlos. There is no knowing at present where this place is located but the terrorist used it to stash weapons. The book may have belonged to the original tenant or to Carlos himself, who I assume must have read it for curiosity value and inspiration, despite its chilling ending. In a 2016 interview, the Jackal described himself as a “professional revolutionary”, stating, “It’s a miracle that I’m still alive, I’ve survived so many operations”. A list of these can be found on Wikipedia. My Budapest Times story “Shadowy Hungarians had role in attempt to kill de Gaulle” can be read here . The three, Lajos Marton, Gyula Sári and László Varga, all came from working class and military backgrounds, and were staunchly anti-communist. They met during the 1956 Uprising in Hungary then went on the run from the occupying authorities and made their ways to France. The attempt by French military personnel to kill de Gaulle in the Paris suburb Petit-Clamart in August 1962 was unsuccessful. Carlos the Jackal, though, could claim many victims and one thing seems sure – there will be no memorial plaques on Rózsadomb anytime soon. https://slguardian.org/polands-welcome-t.text: Father Adrian Mantykiewicz celebrates Mass while still bruised from the assault in Jarosław. Poland’s public mood towards Ukrainian refugees has shifted sharply since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, with opposition to accepting displaced Ukrainians now exceeding support for the first time. Rising hostility, fuelled by political polarisation, historical disputes and online disinformation, has left members of the country’s largest foreign community increasingly anxious about speaking their native language in public. Polish authorities have also warned that Russia is exploiting tensions between the two neighbouring countries to weaken domestic support for Ukraine, even as Warsaw maintains its military and institutional backing for Kyiv. The latest escalation followed a knife attack at a monastery in Jarosław, eastern Poland, in which a priest was killed and four other people were injured. Polish authorities reported that the Ukrainian assailant had suffered an acute psychotic episode. Ukraine’s government immediately condemned the attack, while the Catholic Church appealed for restraint. Adrian Mantykiewicz, one of the injured priests, asked for clemency for the attacker and urged people not to blame an entire nation for the actions of one individual. The appeal did little to calm online hostility. Polish media described an atmosphere close to mob violence on social networks, while the state monitoring centre for disinformation, NASK, reported that expressions of hatred had reached their highest level since July. Pawel Cymbor, a disinformation analyst at Fakenews.pl, said the priest’s appeal changed how some users perceived him. “The homily radically changed attitudes towards the priest on social media, where a section of users went from considering him a victim to labelling him a traitor and a defender of [Stepan] Bandera,” he said. Bandera, a Ukrainian nationalist regarded by some in Ukraine as a national hero, remains a deeply contentious figure in Poland because of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army’s association with massacres in Volhynia and Galicia during the Second World War. For the more than 1.5 million Ukrainians living in Poland, who account for about 4% of the population, the changing atmosphere has affected everyday life. Oleksandra Fedorchuk, a journalist with Slawa, the Ukrainian-language channel of Polish public broadcaster TVP, arrived in Poland in March 2022, shortly after Russia began its full-scale invasion. She now avoids speaking Ukrainian in public. “We avoid speaking Ukrainian in the street and on public transport; it is safer to try to make ourselves invisible,” she said. Dmytro Dymydyuk, who works at Ukrainski Dom, an organisation advising refugees on housing, employment and documentation, has received increasing reports of harassment involving Ukrainian children at school, including incidents involving classmates, teachers and strangers. Although he has not personally experienced abuse, he also avoids speaking his language in public “so as not to provoke the Poles”. “I am not proud of it, but I want to live in peace,” he said. The change is reflected in polling. According to the public opinion research centre CBOS, 91% of Poles supported accepting Ukrainian refugees in April 2022, while only 4% opposed it. By July 2026, opposition had risen to 52%, overtaking the 42% who supported accepting refugees. Meanwhile, the number of reported hate crimes against Ukrainians has increased. According to the Polish newspaper Rzeczpospolita, police received 180 reports of such offences in the first half of 2026, 30% more than in the same period a year earlier. The conflict-monitoring organisation ACLED recorded 13 physical attacks against Ukrainians in Poland between January and the end of August, almost twice the total for all of 2025 and a substantial increase from just one recorded incident in 2024. The deterioration has unfolded alongside renewed disputes over the countries’ shared history. In May, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky awarded an army unit the honorary name “Heroes of the UPA”, referring to the Ukrainian Insurgent Army. In Poland, the organisation is associated with the killings of Polish civilians in Volhynia and Galicia during the Second World War. Polish President Karol Nawrocki responded by withdrawing the Order of the White Eagle, Poland’s highest national distinction, which Zelensky had received in 2023. Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s government also urged Kyiv to reverse the decision, but the controversy continued for weeks without a change in Ukraine’s position. A CBOS survey conducted shortly after the diplomatic dispute found that 46% of Poles viewed bilateral relations negatively, the worst result in the series. Some 65% blamed Ukraine for the poor state of the relationship. The dispute also coincided with a surge in online abuse. According to the Polish Institute of International Affairs (PISM), mentions containing extremely offensive terms directed at Ukrainians increased by 171% between 26 May and 13 July, reaching 364,000. The posts generated 1.2 million reactions, with the institute linking many of them to pro-Russian campaigns. PISM has warned that Moscow benefits from the growing distance between Poland and Ukraine, using propaganda and disinformation to deepen divisions. Cymbor, however, cautioned against attributing anti-Ukrainian sentiment solely to Russian interference. Poland’s highly polarised domestic political environment also provides fertile ground for hostility, he said, while Fakenews.pl has identified numerous actors and disinformation networks operating within the country. A recurring tactic is to amplify crimes suspected of involving Ukrainians and encourage the belief that all Ukrainians should be judged by the actions of individuals. Political decisions have contributed to the changing climate. Tusk condemned attackers who assault people for speaking with a different accent and ordered stronger action against hate crimes, describing perpetrators as acting “in favour of Russia”. Yet his government has also reduced refugee benefits to the point of near elimination. Hanna Machinska, a lawyer and professor at the University of Warsaw, argues that the cuts reinforce negative stereotypes by suggesting Ukrainians are unwilling to work. A recent study by Deloitte and the UN refugee agency, UNHCR, estimated that Ukrainian refugees contributed 2.4% of Poland’s gross domestic product in 2025. Machinska fears the atmosphere will deteriorate further ahead of parliamentary elections scheduled for autumn 2027. At a recent meeting, she recalled, a Ukrainian woman said acquaintances had asked whether she was afraid to travel to Poland. “Afraid to travel to Poland when coming from a country at war! It is a dramatic message,” Machinska said.
